abstract: Dooge asked whether hydrology has laws at the catchment scale. We ask whether a low-dimensional system built under physical laws can match the accuracy of neural networks that outperform process-based models on the same inputs. Three laws constrain a lumped catchment model. Conservation makes it a flux-connected storage network, dissipation fixes the sign of every flux and aggregation determines how the unresolved composition enters the fluxes, through effective laws over threshold distributions and a memory of the forcing. These laws admit four kinds of refinement. A parsimonious model under them, CaRT (11 parameters per catchment), is refined in a loop assisted by AI agents. Each refinement addresses an observed deficit through a hypothesis from the literature. The result, CaRT+, has fourteen states, 35 parameters per catchment and no daily neural network. Most refinements follow from aggregation over thresholds or from variables that carry no water but modulate fluxes. On 602 British and 593 US gauged catchments, single CaRT+ models reach median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.863 and 0.765 in held-out years. A stateful LSTM reaches 0.869 and 0.751 and an entity-aware LSTM 0.862 and 0.754, while three-seed LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003–0.012 in median paired NSE. On 505 drier Australian gauged catchments unused in development, single CaRT+ models reach 0.778 against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs. The results suggest that catchment-scale laws exist as laws of form, with the constitutive families shared and only their parameters learned.

sections.body: The paper asks whether river flow after rain can be predicted by a simple model built under physical laws. Deep-learning models trained on rainfall, temperature and a few catchment properties predict streamflow much better than models built from physical processes. The paper derives three laws: water is conserved, flow runs down gradients and loses energy, and averaging varied land into a few stores leaves a memory of past weather. These laws set how a catchment model may look and how it may be refined. AI agents helped test refinements of a simple model. The result, with no neural network inside, matches deep learning on about 1900 catchments in Britain, the United States and Australia.
sections.heading: Plain Language Summary
sections.headline: Three physical laws constrain catchment models, and a simple model without a neural network matches deep learning on about 1900 catchments.

sections.body: Process-based models have not matched neural networks that use only daily catchment-mean forcing and a few static attributes. It is open whether processes are missing or the laws that combine known processes at catchment scale are missing. The paper tests one fixed, low-dimensional structure with static parameters, and uses the neural network as a measure of the information in the inputs. The strongest differentiable hybrid, a differentiable HBV, is sixteen parallel copies averaged, which is no longer low-dimensional. Training uses 1989–2008, model selection 2009–2010, and the test period 2011–2019 was not used to fit parameters or select checkpoints. The data are 671 CAMELS-GB and 671 CAMELS-US catchments, with 561 CAMELS-AUS catchments not used in development. The comparison includes HBV, a differentiable HBV, a stateful LSTM and an entity-aware LSTM.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Deep-learning models outperform process-based models on streamflow, so the question is whether a low-dimensional structure built under physical laws can match them.

sections.body: This section states three laws that any lumped daily catchment model must satisfy. Conservation says storage changes only through fluxes between stores, so every correction acts on a flux. Dissipation says water flows down the potential, with non-negative conductances, so each flux has the sign of its head difference and an empty store cannot lose water. Aggregation says the lumped flux is the mean of local laws over the possible compositions, and the unresolved composition enters as a memory of the forcing. A corollary gives four admissible refinements: split a volume, add a connection, change the form of a flux law, or modulate a coefficient by the forcing or by conditional variables. Each refinement is meant to nest the model it refines where a natural limit exists. The constitutive families are stated as hypotheses to be tested against observations.
sections.heading: Hydrological laws
sections.headline: Three laws, conservation, dissipation and aggregation, fix the form of a lumped model and admit four kinds of refinement.

sections.body: CaRT has one store for each class that needs a state: soil, quick path and groundwater, together with a routing kernel. It descends from the GR4J family but frees the percolation scale, because the calibrated ratio `K_p`/`K_p,GR4J` ranges over two orders of magnitude (0.11–7.3 between the 10th and 90th percentiles). The GR4J exchange is kept only for losses, since its gain branch violates Law 2 at high storage. Snow is a degree-day store split into five elevation bands, with the parameters `T_T`, CFMAX, SFCF, Γ and `κ_s`. The snowfall correction changes precipitation by a median of less than 0.1 % on CAMELS-GB and CAMELS-US, but by up to about ±30 % in individual CAMELS-US basins. Per-catchment parameters come from a static network with three hidden layers of 128 units, trained on the mean of 1−NSE.
sections.heading: A base model
sections.headline: CaRT, a base model with one store per process class, uses 11 parameters per catchment and is regionalised by a static network.

sections.body: The base model is refined in a loop. A deficit is diagnosed from observations, one refinement is derived from a stated fine-scale assumption, and the refinement is trained with several seeds and compared on a development split. It is kept if it improves the model overall, or improves some classes of catchments without degrading it overall. Diagnostics include seasonal volume bias, the exponent of dry-weather recessions, low-flow volume bias, the event runoff ratio and the sensitivity of melt timing to air temperature. Refinements include a logistic connectivity threshold for the quick release that shifts with soil wetness, a release exponent of 5+k, a viscosity factor, a frost step and a near-stream saturated zone. The resulting CaRT+ has fourteen states, 35 parameters per catchment and seven global constants. AI agents (Claude Code and Codex) executed the loop under the author's instructions and the constraints of the laws.
sections.heading: Refining the base model
sections.headline: Refinements target observed deficits, such as quick-flow connectivity and frost, and each is kept if it improves development-split comparisons.

sections.body: Models are trained on 1989–2008, checkpoints are selected on median NSE over 2009–2010, and the held-out period 2011–2019 is used only for evaluation. Each catchment metric is averaged over three seeds before the median over catchments is reported. Differences are tested with paired per-catchment bootstrap intervals. Benchmarks are HBV, a differentiable HBV, a stateful LSTM and an entity-aware LSTM. Transferred to CAMELS-AUS, CaRT+ is ahead of the stateful LSTM by 0.009 [0.003, 0.015] in the paired median on gauged catchments. However, the LSTM ensemble keeps a lead of 0.010 [0.002, 0.014] over the CaRT+ ensemble. One structural choice, the snow store of CAMELS-GB, was first adopted after its test-period results had been seen, and was confirmed afterwards on the development split.
sections.heading: Results on CAMELS-GB, CAMELS-US and CAMELS-AUS
sections.headline: Single CaRT+ and stateful LSTM models reach 0.863 and 0.869 median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency in Britain, and 0.765 and 0.751 in the United States.

sections.body: As a single model CaRT+ matches a stateful LSTM and an entity-aware LSTM on CAMELS-GB and CAMELS-US, with paired differences in median NSE between −0.004 and +0.008. On the gauged Australian catchments, whose data played no part in deriving the structure, it is ahead of both by 0.009 and 0.014. The authors read the results as support for laws of form: the constitutive families are shared, and what differs between catchments is the parameters. The Budyko relation is described as a law of response rather than of dynamics. The stated limits include the need for soil moisture, groundwater and evaporation observations to constrain the internal states, the dependence of the learned closure on the training climate, and weaker results for three-seed ensembles, low flows and arid held-out catchments.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Known processes assembled under the laws suffice for streamflow accuracy, but the internal states and fluxes still need independent observations.

sections.body: The question was whether a low-dimensional system built under physical laws predicts streamflow as accurately as a neural network on the same inputs. For single models on gauged catchments, CaRT+ has median NSE 0.863 against 0.869 for the stateful LSTM and 0.862 for the EA-LSTM on CAMELS-GB, and 0.765 against 0.751 and 0.754 on CAMELS-US. Three-seed LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003–0.012. On the gauged CAMELS-AUS catchments CaRT+ reaches median NSE 0.778. Removing groups of refinements one at a time shows that runoff generation, quick release and evaporation carry most of the gain. The parameters remained catchment-specific and had to be learned, so the uniqueness of place resides in them.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: One 35-parameter structure matches single LSTMs on 1342 catchments and transfers to 561 Australian ones, supporting laws of form.

sections.body: CAMELS-GB is available from the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, and CAMELS-US from the National Center for Atmospheric Research. The CAMELS-US forcing is Daymet version 4, averaged over the basin polygons, with USGS daily discharge extended to 2019 from the National Water Information System. CAMELS-AUS version 2 is available from Zenodo under record 12575680, release 2.03, and its forcing and attributes are used as distributed. The model code, including CaRT, CaRT+, the HBV, dHBV and LSTM implementations and the fused daily kernels with their adjoints, and the model input files are in the GitHub repository named cartplus under the account xiaxilin.
sections.heading: Open Research
sections.headline: Data sources, an Australian dataset release and the code for CaRT and CaRT+ are listed with their repository and record identifiers.

sections.body: Appendix A treats the composition left unresolved by aggregation. A Taylor expansion gives the instantaneous aggregation error. For a fifth-power law, two units at the mean storage with deviations of plus or minus epsilon give a mean of a s̄^5 (1 + 10ε² + 5ε⁴). The outflow correction is first order in the composition for units in series and vanishes only when the outlet weights are equal. Eliminating the composition gives a functional of the forcing history. Under monotone, compartmental fluxes with a path to the exterior, the initial composition fades. Appendix A.2 gives conditions under which a few states carry this memory exactly or approximately. The last part gives the closed-form daily updates of the stores, the operator splitting used in training, and Table S6, which lists the nested limit of each refinement.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix derives the memory that aggregation leaves, the conditions under which few states carry it, and the daily numerical schemes.
